newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. debate opens amid gloom and frustration.
newsitem.headline: U.N. debate opens amid gloom and frustration.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty (Diplomatic Correspondent)
The United Nations, facing huge debts and a leadership crisis, launched its annual debate on Monday in a sombre mood as countries lined up to appeal for urgent reform of the world body.

"A stalemate persists, an uncomfortable stalemate that leads to a feeling of ... insecurity about the future of the United Nations," Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Palmeira Lampreia told the 185-nation General Assembly.
The annual U.N. assembly session brings together presidents, prime ministers and foreign ministers to discuss conflicts and problems from trade to the environment. The debate lasts three weeks.
With much fanfare, world leaders called for political and financial reforms of the organisation at last year's celebrations to mark the U.N.'s 50th anniversary.
Various committees were set up, but one year later there is no agreement on key reforms and the United Nations is still owed nearly $3 billion in unpaid dues, more than half by the United States.

A U.N. spokeswoman said on Monday that Washington had just paid $40 million, a fraction of what it owes. The United States has demanded faster reforms if it is to pay up, an attitude described on Monday as intimidation by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland.
To the annoyance of many other nations, Washington has also blocked the appointment of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali for the customary second five-year term.
The United States says a more vigorous reformer is needed to lead the United Nations into the 21st century.
Discussions on reforms, including the issue of which countries should become new permanent members of the powerful U.N. Security Council, are bogged down in regional rivalries.
Most countries agree the United Nations must do something to try and restore the brief "golden age" of true cooperation that it enjoyed immediately after the end of the Cold War.

But there is no real agreement about how reform should be achieved, and the United States is in the middle of an election campaign in which the United Nations is regularly vilified by conservative Republicans as an enemy of U.S. interests.

Angola, Argentina, the former Soviet republic of Georgia and others laid out different views on reform in the debate's first session on Monday. U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov speak on Tuesday.
Norway's Brundtland, often mentioned as a potential successor to Boutros-Ghali, said reforms must nevertheless be pushed through to keep the United Nations relevant.
"We are not served by protracted denials of the world as it is," she told the assembly.
"We must go from words of intention to deeds," said Angolan Foreign Minister Venancio de Moura.

There are currently five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council who each have veto power -- the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain. Wealthy Germany and Japan are prime candidates to join them, but there is far less agreement on candidates from the developing world.

The financial crisis has led Boutros-Ghali and others to warn that the United Nations faces bankruptcy. But after the failure of U.N. peacekeeping in Bosnia and Somalia, many countries are now wary of using the institution in conflict resolution -- one factor that could reduce U.N. bills.

One of the few real achievements of the 51st U.N. General Assembly will be the signing of a global treaty banning nuclear tests. The United States, Russia and other nuclear powers are due to sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty on Tuesday, followed by other nations.
However, India's objections to the treaty and its refusal to sign could mean the agreement never enters into force.
